tools.hourly-to-salary-calculator.metada: Convert between hourly wage and annual salary, accounting for vacation time.
tools.hourly-to-salary-calculator.faqs.0: How do I convert hourly wage to annual salary?
Multiply the hourly rate by hours per week, then by weeks per year. $20/hour * 40 hours * 52 weeks = $41,600/year.
tools.hourly-to-salary-calculator.faqs.1: How do I convert annual salary to hourly wage?
Divide the annual salary by the number of work hours per year. Standard 40-hour work week, 52 weeks: $65,000 / 2,080 hours = $31.25/hour.
tools.hourly-to-salary-calculator.faqs.2: Are paid holidays included in the calculation?
If you have paid vacation, use 52 weeks - you're still paid for those weeks. If you only have unpaid vacation, reduce the number of weeks. Most full-time jobs include paid vacation.
tools.hourly-to-salary-calculator.faqs.3: How do taxes affect the conversion?
These calculations are pre-tax (gross income). After-tax (net income) depends on your tax bracket, deductions, and credits. Use a paycheck calculator to estimate after-tax income.

tools.income-tax-calculator.keywords.13: how much tax do I owe
tools.income-tax-calculator.faqs.0.answe: Tax brackets are marginal - only the income within each bracket is taxed at that rate. Being 'in the 24% bracket' does not mean all your income is taxed at 24%. The first $11,925 (single) is taxed at 10%, the next portion at 12%, and so on.
tools.income-tax-calculator.faqs.1.quest: What is the difference between marginal and effective tax rates?
tools.income-tax-calculator.faqs.1.answe: Your marginal tax rate is the bracket your last dollar falls into. Your effective tax rate is total tax divided by total income. Someone earning $85,000 (single) has a marginal rate of 22% but an effective rate of only about 14%.
tools.income-tax-calculator.faqs.2.quest: Should I take the standard deduction or itemize?
tools.income-tax-calculator.faqs.2.answe: Take whichever is larger. The 2026 standard deduction is $15,700 (single) or $31,400 (married). Only itemize if your deductible expenses (mortgage interest, state/local taxes up to $10,000, charitable donations) exceed the standard deduction.

tools.inflation-calculator.faqs.0.questi: Where does the CPI data come from?
tools.inflation-calculator.faqs.0.answer: This calculator uses annual averages of the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. CPI data goes back to 1913 and is updated each year. The reference period is 1982-84 = 100.
tools.inflation-calculator.faqs.1.questi: What is the average inflation rate in the U.S.?
tools.inflation-calculator.faqs.1.answer: From 1913 to 2025, the average annual inflation rate in the U.S. has been about 3.2%. But this varies by decade: the 1970s averaged over 7%, while the 2010s averaged under 2%. Recent years saw a spike reaching 8% in 2022, then cooling to about 2.5% in 2025.
tools.inflation-calculator.faqs.2.questi: How does inflation affect purchasing power?
tools.inflation-calculator.faqs.2.answer: Inflation reduces what each dollar can buy. If inflation is 3% per year, $100 today buys only $97 worth of goods next year. Over 25 years at 3%, $100 loses more than half its purchasing power - you would need about $209 to buy what $100 bought 25 years ago.
tools.inflation-calculator.faqs.3.answer: The 2021-2022 inflation spike was driven by pandemic-era stimulus spending, supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, and energy price increases following geopolitical events. CPI rose 4.7% in 2021 and 8.0% in 2022 - the highest since 1981.
tools.inflation-calculator.faqs.4.questi: Is CPI the only way to measure inflation?
tools.inflation-calculator.faqs.4.answer: No. Other measures include the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index (the Fed's preferred gauge), the Producer Price Index (PPI), and core CPI (excluding volatile food and energy prices). Each captures a different aspect of price changes.
tools.inflation-calculator.faqs.5.questi: How is the inflation adjustment calculated?
tools.inflation-calculator.faqs.5.answer: The formula is: Adjusted Amount = Original Amount * (Target Year CPI / Original Year CPI). For example, $100 in 1990 with a CPI of 130.7, adjusted to 2025 with a CPI of 321.4: $100 * (321.4 / 130.7) = $245.83.

tools.interest-calculator.faqs.0.questio: What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
tools.interest-calculator.faqs.0.answer: Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal: I = P * r * t. Compound interest is calculated on the principal plus accumulated interest, so you earn 'interest on interest'. Over time, compounding grows faster.
tools.interest-calculator.faqs.1.answer: APY (Annual Percentage Yield) is the effective annual rate when compounding is considered. A 5% rate compounded monthly has an APY of 5.12%. APY lets you compare accounts with different compounding frequencies.
tools.interest-calculator.faqs.2.questio: How often should interest be compounded?
tools.interest-calculator.faqs.2.answer: More frequent compounding earns slightly more. $10,000 at 5% for 10 years: monthly compounding = $16,470, annual compounding = $16,289 - a difference of $181. Daily compounding adds even less on top of monthly.

tools.macro-calculator.metadata.descript: Calculate your daily protein, carbs, and fat intake based on your goals, with multiple diet ratio presets.
tools.macro-calculator.faqs.0.question: What are macronutrients?
tools.macro-calculator.faqs.0.answer: Macronutrients (macros) are the three main nutrients that provide calories: protein (4 cal/g), carbohydrates (4 cal/g), and fat (9 cal/g). Tracking macros helps you control body composition, not just total calories.
tools.macro-calculator.faqs.1.question: How much protein do I need?
tools.macro-calculator.faqs.1.answer: For muscle gain: 0.7-1.0 grams per pound of body weight. For maintenance: 0.5-0.7 grams per pound. For fat loss: 0.8-1.2 grams per pound (higher protein preserves muscle during a calorie deficit).
tools.macro-calculator.faqs.2.question: Which macro split should I choose?
tools.macro-calculator.faqs.2.answer: Balanced (30/40/30) works for most people. High protein (40/35/25) is best for muscle gain. Low carb (40/20/40) suits people who feel better on fewer carbs. Keto (30/5/65) is for people adapted to ketosis, with very low carbs.
tools.macro-calculator.faqs.3.question: Do I need to hit my macros exactly?
tools.macro-calculator.faqs.3.answer: No. Hit your protein target within +/- 5 grams (most important), and carbs and fat can be flexible. Hitting your calorie target matters most, followed by protein. Carbs and fat can flex based on preference.

tools.medicaid-work-requirement-calculat: Check if you must meet the new 80-hour work requirement, whether you qualify for an exemption, and what to do next.
What is the Medicaid work requirement?

Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), adults aged 19-64 who joined Medicaid through the ACA expansion must complete 80 hours of qualifying activities per month, such as employment, job training, education, or community service. This takes effect January 1, 2027 for most states, though some states (like Nebraska) are implementing it early. Non-compliance can result in losing Medicaid coverage.
Who is exempt from the Medicaid work requirement?

Mandatory exemptions include: people who are pregnant, parents/caretakers of children 13 or younger, caretakers of people with disabilities, people who are blind, disabled, or medically frail (including those with substance use disorders, serious mental illness, or complex conditions), disabled veterans, American Indians/Alaska Natives, former foster youth under 26, people in substance abuse treatment programs, people already meeting TANF or SNAP work requirements, people currently incarcerated or released within 90 days, and certain Medicare beneficiaries. Additionally, earning at least $580 per month from employment satisfies the requirement through the income-based alternative.
What activities count toward the 80 hours?

Qualifying activities include: paid employment (part-time or full-time), job training or workforce development programs, enrollment in higher education or vocational/technical education (at least half-time), community service or volunteer activities, and participation in work programs. There is also an income-based alternative: earning at least $580 per month satisfies the requirement regardless of hours. Caring for a child under 13 or a disabled family member makes you exempt. 80 hours per month is roughly equivalent to 20 hours per week.
What happens if I don't meet the 80 hours?

If your state cannot verify your compliance, you'll receive a notice and have a 30-day cure period to prove compliance or request an exemption. If you don't respond within 30 days, you'll be disenrolled from Medicaid. To restore coverage, you must reapply from scratch. Importantly, people who lose Medicaid due to work requirement non-compliance are also ineligible for ACA marketplace premium tax credits, meaning you also can't get subsidized health insurance through Healthcare.gov.

The federal mandate takes effect January 1, 2027. However, states can implement the requirement early. Nebraska began enforcement on May 1, 2026. States are required to begin notifying beneficiaries between June 30 and August 31, 2026. HHS must release the full interim final rule by June 1, 2026.
Does this apply in every state?

It applies to all states that have expanded Medicaid (40 states plus Washington, D.C.). The 10 states that have not expanded Medicaid (Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Wisconsin, Wyoming) are not directly affected because they have no Medicaid expansion population. States cannot waive this requirement after January 1, 2027.
Will I permanently lose health insurance?

You will lose Medicaid and must reapply. There is no automatic reinstatement. Additionally, the law bars people disenrolled for non-compliance from receiving ACA marketplace premium tax credits, meaning you may not be able to get affordable health insurance through any subsidized program until you regain Medicaid eligibility. This makes compliance or requesting an exemption extremely important.
How do I report my hours?

States must first try to verify your compliance through automatic data matching (wage records, TANF/SNAP records, education enrollment). If your hours can't be verified automatically, you may need to self-report. Your state Medicaid office will provide specific reporting instructions. States verify compliance at least every 6 months.

Yes. Any paid employment counts toward the 80 monthly hours, including part-time work. If you work 20 hours a week, you meet the requirement. There is no minimum wage or income threshold - only the hours matter.

If you're temporarily unemployed, you can meet the requirement through job training, education (at least half-time), community service, or volunteer activities. You can combine different qualifying activities to reach 80 hours. If you've recently been released from incarceration (within 90 days), you're temporarily exempt.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) was signed into law in 2025 and adds new work requirements for adults who joined Medicaid through the ACA expansion. Starting January 1, 2027, you must complete 80 hours of qualifying activities per month to keep your Medicaid coverage. Some states are implementing this early - Nebraska began enforcement in May 2026.
Who Is Affected and Qualifying Activities

This requirement applies to adults aged 19-64 who joined Medicaid through the expansion program (typically people with income up to 138% of the federal poverty level). About 18.5 million people nationwide are enrolled in expansion Medicaid. You can satisfy the 80-hour requirement through any combination of: paid employment (any job, part-time or full-time), job training (workforce development programs, apprenticeships, or vocational training), higher education or vocational/technical education (must be enrolled at least half-time), and community service (volunteering at nonprofits, faith-based organizations, or government programs). There is also an income-based alternative: earning at least $580 per month (80 hours at the federal minimum wage of $7.25/hour) satisfies the requirement regardless of actual hours worked.

Many people are exempt and don't need to meet the 80-hour requirement. Exemptions include: people who are pregnant or within 12 months postpartum, parents or caretakers of children 13 or younger, caretakers of family members with disabilities, people with disabilities (physical, intellectual, or developmental), people with substance use disorders, serious mental illness, or complex conditions, disabled veterans, American Indians and Alaska Natives, former foster youth under 26, people in substance abuse treatment programs, people already meeting TANF or SNAP work requirements, people currently incarcerated or released within the past 90 days, and certain Medicare beneficiaries. If your state can't verify that you meet the 80-hour requirement, you'll receive a notice. You then have 30 days to prove compliance or request an exemption. If you don't respond, you'll be disenrolled from Medicaid and must reapply from scratch to restore coverage. Importantly, if you lose Medicaid for failing the work requirement, you'll also be barred from premium tax credits for ACA marketplace insurance (Healthcare.gov).
tools.obbba-tax-calculator.metadata.desc: Estimate tax savings from tips, overtime, and more under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
tools.obbba-tax-calculator.faqs.0.answer: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) is a proposed tax legislation that includes tip tax exemptions, overtime pay exemptions, a senior citizen deduction, and an auto loan interest deduction. It aims to reduce the tax burden on working Americans and seniors.
tools.obbba-tax-calculator.faqs.1.questi: How does the tip tax exemption work?
tools.obbba-tax-calculator.faqs.1.answer: OBBA allows service workers to exclude up to $30,000 of tip income (single) or $60,000 (married filing jointly) from taxable income. This applies to workers who receive tips - servers, bartenders, hotel staff.
tools.obbba-tax-calculator.faqs.2.questi: What is the senior citizen deduction?
tools.obbba-tax-calculator.faqs.2.answer: Taxpayers 65 and older can claim an additional standard deduction of up to $6,000 (single) or $12,000 (married filing jointly). This reduces taxable income, directly lowering the tax bill.
tools.obbba-tax-calculator.faqs.3.questi: What is the auto loan interest deduction?
tools.obbba-tax-calculator.faqs.3.answer: OBBA allows deducting up to $10,000 of auto loan interest (available to taxpayers with AGI below $100,000). This applies to individuals purchasing new cars.
